seo.title: AI Audio Research | Igor Szuniewicz
seo.description: Bachelor thesis: Can AI generate real-time sound effects for games?

header.title: Can AI generate game audio in real-time?
header.description: For my bachelor thesis I tried to find out if AI can generate sound effects fast enough for games. I built a Unity prototype that talks to AI models through a Python server. Spoiler: it's not ready yet, but I found a workaround.

setup.title: What I tested and why
setup.intro: Games contain hundreds of pre-recorded sound files. Every shot, footstep, and explosion is a WAV file someone recorded in a studio. AI could generate these on the fly. Every sound would be unique, adapted to the situation, without gigabytes of files. The problem: latency. If a sound arrives even 100ms late, players notice.
setup.approach: I built a prototype. Unity sends requests to a Python server, which calls an AI model and streams back audio. I tested three models: ElevenLabs (cloud API, best quality but latency spikes), MMAudio (video-to-audio model I adapted for games, runs locally), and AudioGen (Meta's text-to-audio, most consistent but still slow).

results.title: Measured Latency
results.subtitle: Generation times for each model compared to what games actually need. Log scale, because the differences are that large.

tooltip.elevenlabs: Cloud API. Best quality, but latency jumps wildly, from 1s to 12s on the same day.
tooltip.mmaudio: Video-to-audio model adapted for games. Runs locally, 2-5s per sound.
tooltip.audiogen: Meta's text-to-audio. Most consistent (~3s), but still too slow for real-time.
tooltip.cached: Pre-generated sounds served from memory. Delivery time 21-55ms.

elevenlabs.note: Cloud-based, quality depends on server load

mmaudio.note: Local, originally designed for video soundtracks

audiogen.note: Most consistent, but 3s is still 3s too slow

solution.title: Caching sounds ahead of time
solution.story: None of the models came close to real-time. The fastest still took over a second, about 60x too slow for a gunshot. I had added a simple cache earlier to avoid generating the same sound twice. Then I noticed the times in the logs: 21-55ms. That's fast enough.
solution.insight: I stopped trying to make AI faster and started thinking about timing instead. Generate sounds during loading screens or quiet moments. Cache them. When a player triggers one, serve it instantly and queue up a replacement in the background.

loading.label: Loading screen
loading.description: AI generates sounds in the background while the player waits

play.label: Player acts
play.description: Sound plays from cache in under 55ms

refill.label: Background refill
refill.description: System generates replacement sounds for next time

solution.usecases: This works best for predictable sounds like ambient audio, cutscene effects, and shots with limited fire rate. It fails for very frequent events like footsteps, where the cache drains faster than AI can refill it.

closing.conclusion: AI audio is not ready to replace traditional game sound design. It's too slow for real-time. But if you cache sounds ahead of time, it can add variety and reduce file sizes for certain use cases.
closing.reflection: The interesting part wasn't which model worked best. It was figuring out that speed doesn't matter if you generate at the right time. Even slow AI works if you call it when nobody's listening.

session2.title: Local AI Testing (It Failed)
session2.content: I tried running MusicGen and AudioLDM2 on student hardware with no GPU. Results: 4-10 seconds per sound. Way too slow for any gameplay that needs fast reactions. Local-only AI generation isn't viable yet.

session4.title: Stress-Testing the Hybrid Approach
session4.content: I combined procedural audio with cloud AI in a hybrid system and pushed it hard: 100 simultaneous requests handled in under 200ms. Hit 2253 generations per second. Procedural path runs at 5ms, cloud path at 2-4 seconds. The hybrid model works for real games.
